description: The poet Ka comes back from years of exile in Germany to Kars, a poor, half-forgotten city in the far north-east of Turkey near the Armenian border, to report on an epidemic of suicides among devout young women, and is snowed in for three days during which a small theatrical coup convulses the town. The real Kars gives the book its bones: the snowbound streets, the theatre where the coup is broadcast live, the tea houses of the unemployed, and the ruined Armenian churches that speak of a vanished past.

title: The Museum of Innocence
author: Orhan Pamuk
description: One man's love turned into an inventory of a city. The map runs from the wealthy boutiques and flats of Nişantaşı, where Kemal is engaged and the affair begins, down the hill through Beyoğlu to the old timber houses of Çukurcuma, where the years of longing settle and where Pamuk later built a real museum to hold them.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
description: Mayfair drawing rooms and the opium dens of the docks, a few miles and an entire moral universe apart. Wilde is precise about the geography of respectability: Lord Henry keeps a house in Curzon Street, Dorian one on Grosvenor Square, and the road to ruin runs east to the quays past Blue Gate Fields.

title: God's Bits of Wood
author: Ousmane Sembène
description: The long railway strike of 1947-48 seen from the line itself. The workshops of Thiès stop, and from there the walkout runs west to the capital and port at Dakar and east along the track to Bamako. When the men are starved back toward defeat, the women take up the fight and march the road from Thiès to Dakar. The map holds the western Senegal stretch of that strike.

title: Crystal Boys
author: Pai Hsien-yung
description: Expelled from home for his sexuality, the young A-Qing joins the hidden community of gay youths who gather after dark in Taipei's New Park, a secret 'kingdom of the night' with its own laws and legends. Pai maps the real city of the early 1970s: New Park with its lotus pond, the bar the outcasts open together, the family homes and military-dependents' villages they are cast out of, and the neon nightlife of Ximending.

title: Texaco
author: Patrick Chamoiseau
description: Marie-Sophie Laborieux tells an urban planner sent to raze her shantytown the whole 150-year history of her family and of Texaco, the improvised quarter she founded on company land above Fort-de-France, from slavery through emancipation to the modern city. Chamoiseau maps the real Martinique: the tin-and-timber quarter of Texaco clinging to the hillside, the city of Fort-de-France below, the plantations of the enslaved past, and old Saint-Pierre before Mont Pelée destroyed it in 1902.

title: Perfume: The Story of a Murderer
author: Patrick Süskind
description: A Paris built from smell before sight: the reeking fish stalls of the old Innocents charnel-ground, the tanneries steaming by the Seine, and a perfumer's shop crowded onto a bridge over the river. The map anchors in the medieval heart of the city, then follows its scent-obsessed foundling south across France to the perfume town of Grasse, marked here as a deliberate excursion beyond Paris.

title: Voss
author: Patrick White
description: In the 1840s the obsessive German explorer Voss sets out to cross the Australian continent, sustained by a strange, wordless spiritual bond with Laura Trevelyan, a young woman he leaves behind in Sydney. White's novel holds together two worlds: colonial Sydney, with the Bonner household and the harbour from which the expedition departs, and the vast unmapped interior, drawn from the real inland journeys of explorers like Leichhardt, where the party is broken and Voss meets his death.

title: The Spider's House
author: Paul Bowles
description: In the ancient Moroccan city of Fez in 1954, as the nationalist rising against French rule reaches the medina, an illiterate boy, Amar, and a disillusioned American writer, Stenham, are thrown together amid the violence. Bowles maps the real city precisely: the labyrinth of Fez el-Bali, the shrine of Moulay Idriss and the Qarawiyyin at its heart, the French Ville Nouvelle where the settlers live, the Palais Jamaï on the medina's edge, and the Merinid tombs on the hills above from which the whole city is seen.

title: The Ventriloquist's Tale
author: Pauline Melville
description: A century of one Wapishana family plays out across the Rupununi, the vast grass plain of southern Guyana between the Kanuku Mountains and the Brazilian border. Ranches and a Jesuit mission sit among the savannah settlements around Lethem, while a modern thread carries a son of the family north to the coastal capital, Georgetown, some four hundred kilometres away.

title: The Good Earth
author: Pearl S. Buck
description: Wang Lung, a poor farmer, rises through his devotion to the land, marrying the plain, steadfast slave O-lan, until famine drives the family south to a great city and back, and returning fortune lifts them into a wealth that draws the next generation away from the soil that made them. Buck kept her geography deliberately broad, but rooted it in the real farming country of eastern China she knew: the fields and the great landlord's house, and the southern city where the starving family scatters in the streets.

title: Mine Boy
author: Peter Abrahams
description: Xuma comes from the north to work in the gold mines of Johannesburg and lodges in the crowded slum of Malay Camp, where he slowly wakes to the injustice of the colour bar that rules every hour of his life. Abrahams maps the real segregated city: the multiracial shebeen world of Malay Camp and Vrededorp, the deep gold mines and their white dumps south of town, the white city centre where black men are only ever labour, and the streets where the police raid and the new consciousness stirs.

title: Miss Smilla's Feeling for Snow
author: Peter Høeg
description: Smilla Jaspersen, a prickly half-Inuit Greenlander in Copenhagen with an expert's feeling for ice and snow, refuses to believe that the small Greenlandic boy from her building simply fell to his death, and her investigation uncovers a secret mining conspiracy that draws her onto a ship bound for a remote Greenland glacier. Høeg's thriller maps a real geography: the wintry Copenhagen of the harbour and the cryolite company, the voyage north across the Atlantic, and the ice of Greenland that is Smilla's true element.

title: Smilla's Sense of Snow
author: Peter Høeg
description: A Copenhagen of black winter water and Greenlandic exile. A half-Inuit woman who reads snow the way others read print refuses to accept that a neighbour's child simply fell from a warehouse roof, and follows the cold trail from the flats of Christianshavn out through the harbour and the Freeport to a ship bound north. The map runs along the Inner Harbour waterfront and up the Østerbro shore.

title: This Earth of Mankind
author: Pramoedya Ananta Toer
description: Colonial Surabaya at the turn of the twentieth century, the largest port of the Dutch East Indies and a city ruled by a strict ladder of race and law. A gifted Javanese student at the elite Dutch H.B.S. is pulled south to Wonokromo, into the household of a formidable concubine who runs a European farm, and finally into the colonial courts. The map runs from the old town on the Kalimas down through Wonokromo to the sugar country of East Java.

title: Fortress Besieged
author: Qian Zhongshu
description: Qian Zhongshu's great comic novel follows Fang Hongjian, home from Europe with a bought diploma, through the pretensions of 1930s Shanghai society, a farcical journey to a shabby university in the interior, and a marriage that proves the book's famous image: a besieged fortress, which those outside want to storm and those inside want to escape. The city anchors it, its returning ships, salons and matchmaking, before the long trek inland and the disillusioned return.

title: The Dark Side of Love
author: Rafik Schami
description: Schami's vast Damascene saga braids a forbidden love across a blood feud between two clans with a murder mystery and a century of Syrian history. Old Damascus is its heart: the Christian quarter of Bab Touma where the clans live, the ancient Straight Street running through the walled city, the Umayyad Mosque at its centre, and the shadow of the secret police; the feud reaches back to the mountain village of Mala from which both families came.

title: Invisible Man
author: Ralph Ellison
description: The narrator's Harlem: a stretch of Lenox Avenue and 125th Street where he speaks for the Brotherhood, sees an old couple evicted onto the pavement, and is finally swept into a night of fire and looting. The arc runs from a Southern college and a downtown paint works into the heart of Harlem and down to the forgotten cellar where a man who feels unseen retreats underground.

title: Prisión Verde
author: Ramón Amaya Amador
description: The banana zone of Honduras's Caribbean lowlands in the 1930s, where the fruit companies ran the Sula valley as a private domain. The map follows the campeños from the endless plantation rows and company camps around El Progreso, along the Ulúa river, out to the industrial city of San Pedro Sula and the export port of Tela.

title: De Niro's Game
author: Rawi Hage
description: Rawi Hage's Beirut is the Christian East of the 1980s civil war: the tight streets of Achrafieh, the militia checkpoints and rooftop gunners, the port and the coast road north to the casino, all pressed against the Green Line that split the city from downtown south to the National Museum. The map runs from that dividing line across East Beirut to the harbour, then follows Bassam's flight out of the country.

title: Vilnius Poker
author: Ričardas Gavelis
description: The Soviet-era Vilnius of a paranoid mind: the capital of occupied Lithuania in the 1970s, its baroque Old Town, its library and its river all watched and warped by an unseen 'Them'. The map holds to the historic centre, from the university library and Cathedral Square up the castle hill to Gediminas Avenue, then renamed for Lenin, and the bend of the Neris.

title: How Green Was My Valley
author: Richard Llewellyn
description: The narrator Huw Morgan remembers his childhood in a South Wales coal-mining valley, in a close chapel-going community that the growing slag heap and the souring of the pits slowly destroy. Llewellyn set his idealised valley in the Rhondda, around Gilfach Goch: the terraced village and the Morgan house, the colliery that pays and kills, the slag tip creeping down the mountain to bury the green, the chapel at the moral centre, and the mountain top that survives above it all.

title: Native Son
author: Richard Wright
description: In 1930s Chicago, a young Black man crosses the hard color line from the crowded South Side Black Belt into a rich white household in Hyde Park, and one panicked night sets the machinery of the city against him.

title: Kidnapped
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
description: David Balfour's road runs the width of Scotland in the year after the '45: from the House of Shaws by Cramond, out to the brig at Queensferry, wrecked on the reefs off Erraid by Mull, then east on foot through Appin and across the deserts of Rannoch back to Edinburgh. Almost every place is real and named, tied to the true Appin Murder of 1752; the bbox spans the whole crossing, Edinburgh west to Erraid.

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
description: The respectable Dr Jekyll brews a potion that frees his hidden appetites as the monstrous Mr Hyde, and the lawyer Utterson traces the growing horror through a fog-bound London toward a locked cabinet and a confession. Stevenson's city is a real, gaslit London of double lives: the fine house with its sinister back door, the squalid Soho lodgings of Hyde, and the lanes where his violence erupts, all mapping the divided self onto the divided town.

title: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
description: Stevenson keeps the geography deliberately shadowy, but the districts are real. Hyde's sinister side-door opens on a by-street near Soho; the same building is Dr Jekyll's handsome house around the corner in a West End square; Dr Lanyon holds court in Cavendish Square, the citadel of medicine; Hyde keeps rooms in Soho; and Sir Danvers Carew is beaten to death by night in a lane near the river at Westminster. The named districts are exact; the exact doors are composite, which is what the labels are for.

title: The Man Without Qualities
author: Robert Musil
description: Musil's Vienna is the capital of a monarchy he nicknames Kakania, in its last year before the war that will end it. A detached young man drifts through the salons and ministries of an empire busy planning a grand patriotic jubilee that history will never let it hold. The map runs from the Ringstrasse and the imperial Hofburg through the palais quarter of the inner city out to the baroque garden districts where he keeps a small house of his own.

author: Roberto Bolaño
description: Bolaño's Santa Teresa is a thin fictional mask over Ciudad Juárez, the Mexican border city facing El Paso across the Rio Grande. The map runs from the international bridges and the old downtown out to the maquiladora factories and the desert lots on the city's edge, where over years the bodies of hundreds of murdered women were found. A European frame, followed here to Bremen, opens the book far from that violence.

title: A Fine Balance
author: Rohinton Mistry
description: Mistry never names the city by the sea, but its stations, promenade and slums are unmistakably 1970s Bombay, today's Mumbai. Under the 1975-77 Emergency the map runs from a great railway terminus and a seafront drive out to the pavement stretches and the bulldozed slum colony where two tailors, fleeing caste violence in an inland village, try to hold a life together.

title: Robbery Under Arms
author: Rolf Boldrewood
description: The bushranging and gold-rush country of colonial New South Wales, and the long ride south to Melbourne. Boldrewood (Thomas Alexander Browne) drew the Turon diggings, the cattle runs, and the rugged ranges from a lifetime in the bush. The Marstons' hidden valley, "Terrible Hollow", is invented, but it is set in real country and the Turon, Bathurst, the Weddin Mountains, and Melbourne are all on the map. It brings a whole continent, Australia, into the atlas.

title: Doña Bárbara
author: Rómulo Gallegos
description: The flooded savannah of Apure, where a Caracas lawyer comes home to a cattle ranch on the Arauca and finds a neighbour who has been swallowing his land. The map runs from the provincial capital and seat of law at San Fernando de Apure west across the open llanos to the great river, with the two rival ranches set among the plains between them.

title: Kim
author: Rudyard Kipling
description: It opens on the gun Zam-Zammah outside the Lahore Museum, both still there, then walks the Grand Trunk Road the length of northern India. The anchor city is Lahore, now in Pakistan; the road and the Great Game carry the book east to Benares and north into the Himalayan foothills, so the bounding box spans the whole run from the Punjab to the Ganges.

title: Midnight's Children
author: Salman Rushdie
description: Saleem Sinai, born on the stroke of India's independence, tells his life and the nation's together, from a Kashmir lake in 1915 through his Bombay childhood on Warden Road to the ghettos of Old Delhi and the swamps of the 1971 war. The anchor is Bombay; the story reaches the length of the subcontinent.

title: Midnight's Children
author: Salman Rushdie
description: Saleem Sinai's Bombay, from Independence in 1947 to the Emergency of the mid-1970s, seen mostly from the hillside villas of Methwold's Estate on the Warden Road rise. The map holds to the elite crescent of Malabar Hill, Breach Candy and Cumballa Hill, with the school in the Fort and the sea at Chowpatty; the family saga's far excursions to Kashmir, Delhi, Karachi and the Sundarbans sit outside this frame.

title: The Moor's Last Sigh
author: Salman Rushdie
description: Moraes 'Moor' Zogoiby narrates the fall of his family, the fabulously mixed da Gama-Zogoiby spice dynasty of Cochin, from the pepper warehouses and the old Jewish quarter of Mattancherry to the art and gangland of Bombay, and at last to an exile in Andalusia that rhymes with the fall of Moorish Granada. Rushdie roots the saga in a real south India: the spice trade of Cochin, the Paradesi synagogue, the harbour of Vasco da Gama's landfall, and the far cities to which the family's ruin carries the Moor.

title: The Satanic Verses
author: Salman Rushdie
description: Two Indian actors survive the mid-air explosion of a hijacked jet, fall onto an English beach transformed into angel and devil, and are pulled through Thatcher-era London and its immigrant East End as their fortunes and identities come apart.

title: Girl at War
author: Sara Nović
description: The Croatia of the war for independence and of the peace that follows it. The map opens in Zagreb in 1991, a ten-year-old's city of air-raid sirens, shelters and a family flat, then runs south to the killing grounds near the Bosnian border and, a decade on, back to the Dalmatian coast where the narrator returns to face what happened.

title: Our Lady of the Nile
author: Scholastique Mukasonga
description: An elite Catholic girls' lycee perched high in the mountains of southern Rwanda, close to a spring held to be a source of the Nile. Behind the convent order and the school routine, the Hutu quotas and Tutsi persecution of the wider country play out among the pupils, a rehearsal in miniature for the genocide still to come. The map runs from the forested highlands near the Nile source down to the town of Butare and out to the capital, Kigali.

title: Divine Punishment
author: Sergio Ramírez
description: The provincial León of the early Somoza years, mapped through a sensational poisoning trial: a compact colonial grid of cathedral and plaza, courthouse and pharmacy, the grand houses of the local elite and the railway station that ties the town to the coast. Ramírez maps a real city, and the map keeps to its streets.

title: Border Town
author: Shen Congwen
description: Shen Congwen's lyrical pastoral is set in the little ferry town of Chadong, on a river in the far west of Hunan near the borders of Sichuan and Guizhou, where the orphan girl Cuicui lives with her grandfather, the old ferryman, and comes shyly of age between two brothers who both love her. The real West Hunan landscape is the whole book: the rope ferry over the green stream, the white pagoda above it, the little riverside town and its dragon-boat festival, and the encircling hills.

title: Silence
author: Shusaku Endo
description: The Nagasaki coast in the 1640s, during the shogunate's campaign to stamp out Christianity. Two Portuguese Jesuits land in secret and shelter with the hidden Christians of the Sotome fishing villages and the offshore Goto Islands, before capture carries them to the city, its magistrate and the fumie. The map runs from the Sotome shore north of the city, out to the Goto Islands, and into Nagasaki itself.

title: Kristin Lavransdatter
author: Sigrid Undset
description: In fourteenth-century Norway, Kristin, daughter of the landowner Lavrans in the Gudbrandsdal valley, defies her betrothal for a passionate, ruinous love, and lives out a long life of desire, guilt, motherhood and faith that ends amid the Black Death. Undset's Nobel-winning trilogy maps a real medieval Norway: the valley farm of Kristin's childhood, the cathedral city of Nidaros where she seeks absolution, the convent at Oslo, and her husband's estate in Trøndelag.

title: Savushun
author: Simin Daneshvar
description: In Shiraz during the Allied occupation of Iran in the Second World War, Zari watches her idealistic landowner husband Yusof refuse to sell his grain to the foreign army while famine and intrigue close in around their family. The first novel by an Iranian woman, and one of the most beloved in Persian, Daneshvar's Savushun maps a real Fars: the city and the family house and garden, the estates and villages Yusof will not betray, the restless tribes, and the mourning that gives the book its name.

title: Purge
author: Sofi Oksanen
description: A farmhouse in rural western Estonia, the woods around it, and the country town beyond, held across the decades from the deportations of the 1940s to the first free summer of 1992. From this Laanemaa yard the story pulls east to Tallinn and, in the trafficking chapters, out of the country altogether.

title: The Charterhouse of Parma
author: Stendhal
description: A young nobleman crosses Napoleonic Europe and the intrigues of a tiny Italian court. The map runs across northern Italy: Milan under the French, the family castle on Lake Como, and the little despotic state of Parma with its citadel prison, where the story ends in a monastery. One scene falls far outside the setting, at Waterloo in Belgium, where the hero wanders the battle without ever grasping it.

title: The Red and the Black
author: Stendhal
description: The carpenter's son Julien Sorel, brilliant, proud and ambitious in a France where the army's red is closed to him and only the church's black offers a poor man a ladder, climbs through hypocrisy and seduction toward a ruin of his own making. Stendhal maps a real Restoration France: the provincial town of Verrières in the Franche-Comté, the seminary at Besançon, and the aristocratic Paris where Julien's rise and fall play out.

title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
author: Stieg Larsson
description: Larsson's Stockholm is a city of investigative journalism and cold money, centred on Södermalm: the Millennium magazine on Götgatan, a reporter's attic on Bellmansgatan, a hacker's flat above Mosebacke. From there the story makes one long excursion north, to the invented island of Hedeby in the river country beyond Gävle, and back again to settle scores in the capital's finance world.

title: The Bell Jar
author: Sylvia Plath
description: Esther Greenwood spends a glittering, hollow month as a guest editor at a women's magazine in New York, staying at a women-only hotel and going through the motions of a life she cannot feel, before returning to her mother's house in the Boston suburbs and a breakdown. The New York half is closely mapped: the Amazon hotel is the real Barbizon, the magazine is Plath's own Mademoiselle, and the United Nations turns up on a date. The Massachusetts scenes of home and hospital run outside the setting.

title: A Golden Age
author: Tahmima Anam
description: Dhaka in 1971, then the capital of East Pakistan, as the Bangladesh Liberation War begins. A widow and her grown children are drawn into the fight from a family house in the planned district of Dhanmondi, past the university where the March crackdown starts, out along the refugee road to Calcutta and a guerrilla camp near the border.

title: The Garden of Evening Mists
author: Tan Twan Eng
description: The Cameron Highlands are Malaysia's cool tea country, a hill station of mist, jungle and terraced estates high in Pahang. A survivor of a wartime Japanese camp comes here to build a garden for her dead sister and instead apprentices to a Japanese gardener, while the Malayan Emergency simmers in the surrounding forest. The map runs from the town of Tanah Rata out across the tea slopes to the mossy summit forest, with the frame narrator's Kuala Lumpur far below.

title: The Gift of Rain
author: Tan Twan Eng
description: On the island of Penang, the half-English, half-Chinese Philip Hutton is taken as a pupil by the Japanese diplomat Endo-san, who teaches him aiki-jutsu and a hard code of duty, only for the bond to be tested to breaking when Japan invades Malaya in 1941. Tan maps his home island: the Hutton family's George Town mansion and the colonial society of the port, the small island off the coast where Endo-san lives and teaches, the town under brutal occupation, and Penang Hill above it all.

title: Season of Migration to the North
author: Tayeb Salih
description: A small village on the great bend of the Nile in northern Sudan, in Salih's own home country near Karmakol and the town of Ad-Dabbah. The narrator comes back from years of study in England to the palms, the water-wheels and the river of his childhood, and finds a stranger, Mustafa Sa'eed, whose buried life in 1920s London shadows the whole book. The map runs along the Dongola reach of the Nile and south to Khartoum, with one deliberate excursion north to the England of the flashback.

title: The Financier
author: Theodore Dreiser
description: Philadelphia and the making of a financier. Dreiser builds Frank Cowperwood's rise and ruin out of the real ledgers of the city: the banks and brokerages of Third Street, the trading floor of the exchange, the municipal offices in Independence Hall he corrupts, and the great gray penitentiary on Fairmount where he is jailed. It brings Philadelphia into the atlas.

title: Jude the Obscure
author: Thomas Hardy
description: The stonemason Jude Fawley dreams of the university, but poverty, class and a doomed love for his free-thinking cousin Sue Bridehead break every hope, in Hardy's bleakest and most controversial novel. It maps his Wessex, drawn from real country: the village of his boyhood, the closed golden city of Christminster that will not have him, and the cathedral towns where he and Sue try and fail to live outside the rules.

title: Tess of the d'Urbervilles
author: Thomas Hardy
description: When her poor family learns it descends from the noble d'Urbervilles, Tess Durbeyfield is sent to claim kin, is seduced and ruined by Alec, and later loves and loses the high-minded Angel Clare, driven at last to murder and the gallows. Hardy sets the tragedy across his Wessex, drawn faithfully from real Dorset: the vale of Tess's village, the d'Urberville estate, the rich dairy country where she finds love, the bleak upland farm of her suffering, and Stonehenge, where she is taken at dawn.

title: The Mayor of Casterbridge
author: Thomas Hardy
description: Hardy's Casterbridge is Dorchester barely disguised: the Roman amphitheatre at Maumbury Rings where Henchard keeps his furtive meetings, the King's Arms on the High Street where the mayor holds his banquet, the corn-market where a hay-trusser who once sold his wife at a country fair has risen to preside, the Ten Hatches weir on the Frome where he goes to drown. Hardy mapped his home town so exactly he later published the keys. Only Weydon-Priors, drawn from Weyhill in Hampshire, sits well outside the town.

title: Buddenbrooks
author: Thomas Mann
description: A Hanseatic grain-merchant family declines over four generations in a Baltic city Mann never names but rebuilds street by street. It is unmistakably his native Lübeck: the family's grand house on Mengstraße, the Marienkirche where they worship, the Holstentor and the quays along the Trave, and Travemünde at the river mouth where Tony holidays. The map runs from the old-town islands north-east to the Baltic resort, and brings Germany into the atlas.

title: Death in Venice
author: Thomas Mann
description: An ageing German writer travels south for rest and is caught by the beauty of a boy he never speaks to, staying on as a cholera the city hushes up spreads through the summer. The map crosses the lagoon from the San Marco waterfront to the Lido, the barrier island of grand hotels and sea baths, and back into the sultry, sirocco-laden alleys of the old city.

title: The Magic Mountain
author: Thomas Mann
description: A young engineer goes up to Davos for a three-week visit to his cousin at a mountain sanatorium and stays seven years, the fever of the place and of one guest keeping him on the heights while the flatland forgets him. The map climbs from the cure-town of Davos-Platz in the valley up the funicular to the sanatorium shelf, and out onto the high slopes where a blizzard nearly ends him.

title: Cloudstreet
author: Tim Winton
description: Two rural families, the Pickles and the Lambs, wash up together in a big rambling house in working-class inner Perth and share it for twenty years. The map runs from the Lambs' lost country home in the south-west, into the shared house and its shop in the western suburbs, out to the wartime city on Perth Water, and always back to the Swan River, where a boy drowns at the start and is made whole at the end.

title: The Bonfire of the Vanities
author: Tom Wolfe
description: Wolfe's panorama of 1980s New York runs on the distance between its worlds. Sherman McCoy, a Wall Street bond trader who thinks of himself as a Master of the Universe, lives in a Park Avenue duplex and takes a wrong turn off the expressway into the South Bronx, where his mistress hits a young Black man with his car. The fallout pulls in the Bronx County Courthouse, a Harlem preacher, and the tabloids, and the map is the city's fault lines laid end to end.

title: Beloved
author: Toni Morrison
description: A house on the free side of the Ohio River, haunted by a mother's choice under slavery. The map runs from the Kentucky plantation of the past, across the river into Ohio, out to a house and a clearing on the northern edge of Cincinnati, and back to the downtown riverfront where the real case behind the novel unfolded.

title: Song of Solomon
author: Toni Morrison
description: A well-off Black man raised in an unnamed Michigan city modeled on Detroit leaves his father's respectable house and travels south to Pennsylvania and Virginia, unearthing a family history that ends in a legend of a flying African.

title: Nervous Conditions
author: Tsitsi Dangarembga
description: The eastern highlands of colonial Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe. A Shona girl's world runs between the family homestead in the Manicaland communal lands, by the Nyamarira, and the town of Umtali twenty miles off, renamed Mutare after independence. Between them lie the trading store and bus route, the mission school her uncle runs, and, far to the west, a convent that promises escape. Rusape and Mutare, the two real towns that frame the region, sit about ninety kilometres apart.

title: The Name of the Rose
author: Umberto Eco
description: In 1327 the Franciscan friar William of Baskerville and his young novice Adso arrive at a rich Benedictine abbey in the mountains of northern Italy, where a series of deaths draws them into a labyrinthine library and a deadly secret about a forbidden book. Eco sets his medieval murder mystery at an unnamed monastery in the Ligurian Apennines: the scriptorium where the monks illuminate manuscripts, the great fortress-library of the Aedificium, the church and grounds, and the Inquisition that arrives to twist the search for truth.

title: The Jungle
author: Upton Sinclair
description: A Lithuanian immigrant and his family come to Chicago for work and are ground down by the meatpacking industry. The map runs across the South Side: the real Union Stock Yards and the packinghouse district called Packingtown, the immigrant slum of Back of the Yards beside it, the dump and fertilizer works on its edge, and the downtown Loop where the ruined hero drifts at the end. Sinclair reported from the yards in 1904 before writing the book.

title: A Bend in the River
author: V. S. Naipaul
description: Salim, a Muslim of Indian descent, buys a shop in a town at a bend of the great river in the interior of a newly independent central African country, and watches the fragile post-colonial order rise and rot under the rule of the Big Man. Naipaul's unnamed town is drawn from Kisangani on the Congo: the river and its choking water hyacinths, the market and the shop, the Big Man's shiny new Domain on the edge of the bush, and the far-off capital from which power and terror flow.

title: A House for Mr Biswas
author: V. S. Naipaul
description: One man's lifelong search for a house of his own, across colonial Trinidad. The map runs from the sugar country of Caroni where Mohun Biswas is born, through the market town of Chaguanas and the family compound he marries into, to the capital, Port of Spain, and the small house in St James that is finally his.

title: In the Shadow of the Banyan
author: Vaddey Ratner
description: The novel opens in Phnom Penh, where a seven-year-old girl of the royal family lives in comfort until, on 17 April 1975, the Khmer Rouge take the city and drive its whole population into the countryside at gunpoint. From there the map runs northwest, along the roads and rivers of the exodus into the rice provinces of Pursat and Battambang, where the family is broken apart by forced labour, hunger and killing. Ratner deliberately leaves her villages unnamed, so the rural points here mark the real region the deportations emptied into, not addresses the book supplies.

title: Under the North Star
author: Väinö Linna
description: In the Häme village of Pentinkulma, the tenant farmer Jussi Koskela clears a bog into a croft, and over three generations the simmering injustice between landless crofters and their landlords swells into the catastrophe of the 1918 Finnish Civil War, which tears the community apart. Linna's national trilogy is rooted in the real countryside of southern Finland he came from: the reclaimed farmland, the parsonage and manor, the workers' hall, and the front and reprisals of the war that split the young nation.

title: Life and Fate
author: Vasily Grossman
description: Grossman's vast novel turns on the Battle of Stalingrad in 1942–43 and braids it with the two great terrors of the century, the Nazi camps and Stalin's own. The city on the Volga is the fixed centre: the ruined streets, the encircled strongpoint the novel calls House 6/1, and the height of Mamayev Kurgan fought over yard by yard. Beyond it the book reaches to the Berdichev ghetto, where the physicist Shtrum's mother writes her last letter, and to the Lubyanka in Moscow, so that the war and the two tyrannies are held in one frame.

title: Z
author: Vassilis Vassilikos
description: A thinly fictionalised account of the 1963 murder of the leftist deputy Grigoris Lambrakis in Thessaloniki by right-wing thugs with police collusion, and the dogged investigation that exposed the conspiracy. Vassilikos maps the real city: the hall where the Deputy speaks at a peace rally, the central street where a three-wheeled truck runs him down, the hospital where he dies, the courthouse where an honest magistrate unpicks the cover-up, and the waterfront under the shadow of the coming junta.

title: Les Misérables
author: Victor Hugo
description: Hugo's Paris is the heart of the book, and he maps it street by street: the Gorbeau tenement on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital, the Luxembourg where Marius and Cosette fall in love, the convent of Petit-Picpus, the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie by Les Halles, and the sewers Valjean carries the wounded Marius through. The story reaches it from far off, though: from Digne in the Alps, from Montreuil-sur-Mer in the north, from the battlefield of Waterloo.

title: Notre-Dame de Paris
author: Victor Hugo
description: A novel written to save a building, and it worked. Hugo's Paris of 1482 is rebuilt street by street around the cathedral on the Île de la Cité, and every place the story turns on is real: the Place de Grève where Esmeralda dances, the Palais de Justice, the thieves' Cour des Miracles, the Bastille, the gibbet at Montfaucon. The cathedral itself has burned and been rebuilt since he wrote it.

title: The Hunchback of Notre-Dame
author: Victor Hugo
description: In the Paris of 1482, the deformed bellringer Quasimodo, the archdeacon Frollo consumed by his desire for the gypsy dancer Esmeralda, and the cathedral itself are bound together in a tragedy of love, cruelty and sanctuary. Hugo's Paris is a real medieval city rendered in vast detail: Notre-Dame above all, the Place de Grève with its pillory and gibbet, the thieves' Court of Miracles, and the Montfaucon gallows where the story ends.

title: Paranoia
author: Viktor Martinovich
description: A thinly veiled authoritarian Belarus, watched from every corner. A young writer's affair with the mistress of the state security minister plays out along the vast Stalinist spine of Independence Avenue, across Independence Square, in the shadow of the security headquarters, and by the slow curve of the Svislach. The map runs south to north through the centre of a real, surveilled Minsk.

title: The Aeneid
author: Virgil
description: A Trojan refugee carries the survivors of a burning city west across the Mediterranean, is nearly held in Carthage by love, and fights his way into Latium to found the line that will become Rome; the poem's destination is the real hill Rome grew on, though its founding is legend.

title: Mrs Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
description: A single Wednesday in mid-June 1923. The novel is ordered by the striking of clocks.

title: To the Lighthouse
author: Virginia Woolf
description: Woolf names the Isle of Skye, but the house, the bay and the lighthouse are drawn entirely from St Ives, Cornwall, where the Stephen family spent childhood summers. The map runs from Talland House, the Woolfs' real holiday home above the town, out across St Ives Bay to Godrevy Lighthouse, the light the children could see from the garden and the one the family in the novel longs to reach.

title: Alamut
author: Vladimir Bartol
description: In eleventh-century Persia, Hasan-i Sabbah, the Old Man of the Mountain, builds the sect of the Assassins at the fortress of Alamut, and makes his young fedayeen die on command by convincing them, through a hidden garden of drugged pleasures, that he can send them to paradise and back. Bartol sets it at the real crag of Alamut in the Alborz mountains: the fortress itself, the secret gardens behind it, the training grounds of the fedayeen, and the roads down which the assassins are sent against the great men of the age.

title: Lolita
author: Vladimir Nabokov
description: A European emigre's obsession with a twelve-year-old girl carries them from a New England town through two years of American motels, a cross-country flight along the highways, and a final murder, all narrated from a prison cell.

title: Pale Fire
author: Vladimir Nabokov
description: A 999-line poem by a New England poet comes wrapped in the mad commentary of his neighbour, who reads into it the story of a deposed king from an imaginary northern land; the real ground beneath it is Nabokov's Cornell and the town of Ithaca.

title: The Purple Land
author: W. H. Hudson
description: Richard Lamb loose in the Banda Oriental, the purple land east of the river: he lands at Montevideo, rides north through Canelones and Florida toward an estancia on the Paysandú border, and is swept into Santa Coloma's doomed revolt across the Cuchilla Grande and the coast of Rocha. Hudson rode this ground himself, and it brings Uruguay, and South America, into the atlas.

title: Death Comes for the Archbishop
author: Willa Cather
description: Archbishop Latour's New Mexico Territory of the 1850s, from the plaza and the cathedral he raises at Santa Fé, out to the sky-city of Ácoma on its mesa, up to rebel Taos and down through Albuquerque. Cather names the real pueblos, towns and missions; the bbox spans northern New Mexico from Ácoma and Albuquerque up to Taos.

title: Absalom, Absalom!
author: William Faulkner
description: Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County is drawn from the real Lafayette County, Mississippi, and its county seat, Jefferson, from Oxford, the town where Faulkner lived and is buried. This novel maps the rise and ruin of Thomas Sutpen: his plantation twelve miles out in the county, the town that watched him, and the graves he left. Much of the story is told and retold decades later, some of it from a cold room at Harvard, so the map runs from the courthouse square out into the county and once far north to Cambridge.

title: The Sound and the Fury
author: William Faulkner
description: The fall of the Compsons, an old Mississippi family, told four times over across three days in 1928 and one in 1910. Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County is drawn from the real Lafayette County, and its town of Jefferson from Oxford, where he lived and is buried. The map grounds the invented county in that ground: the courthouse square, the Compson place, the pasture sold off to a golf course, the branch below it. Quentin's day belongs elsewhere, at Harvard and on the Charles River in Cambridge, Massachusetts, mapped as scenes outside the setting.

title: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
author: William Kamkwamba & Bryan Mealer
description: The maize country of central Malawi, where the Kasungu plateau rolls east from the district town toward the trading centre of Wimbe. Through the 2001-02 famine a teenager on his family's farm teaches himself from library books and builds a windmill out of scrap, turning wind into light and water. The map runs from the farm and the little school at Wimbe out to the district town, and finally south to the capital.

title: Vanity Fair
author: William Makepeace Thackeray
description: The penniless, ruthless Becky Sharp claws her way up through Regency society while her gentle schoolfellow Amelia Sedley suffers for her constancy, in Thackeray's panorama of a world where everything and everyone is for sale. The novel maps a real geography: the London of Russell Square and Mayfair, the Brussels of the ball on the eve of Waterloo, the battlefield itself, and the German spa town where the long story finds its close.

title: The Stolen Bicycle
author: Wu Ming-Yi
description: A writer's hunt for his vanished father's lost bicycle becomes a walk back through twentieth-century Taiwan. The map centres on old central Taipei: Zhonghua Road and the vast Zhonghua Shopping Bazaar the family lived and tailored suits in, and the Wanhua-Bangka district of temples, antique stalls and bicycle shops. The search reaches back to the Japanese colonial years and, far to the south-west, to the forests of the Burma campaign of the Second World War.

title: Homegoing
author: Yaa Gyasi
description: Two half-sisters born in the eighteenth-century Gold Coast never meet, and the novel follows their descendants down parallel lines for two hundred and fifty years. One line stays in the Fante and Asante country of what is now Ghana, anchored on Cape Coast and its slave castle; the other is shipped across the Atlantic into American slavery and, generations later, the Great Migration north. The map centres on the Cape Coast Castle, where the two lines split, and runs inland to the Asante capital at Kumasi.

title: Life of Pi
author: Yann Martel
description: Pi Patel grows up in the French-colonial town of Pondicherry, on India's south-eastern coast, where his father keeps a zoo set among the alleys and beds of the old Botanical Garden. When the family decides to emigrate they sail from Madras, and the story is later told to a visitor in Canada. The map anchors the Indian childhood: the garden, the White Town quarter and the port of departure.

title: Snow Country
author: Yasunari Kawabata
description: Kawabata's snow country is a hot-spring town on the west side of Honshu, reached from Tokyo by a train that runs south to north through a long mountain tunnel and comes out into deep Niigata snow. The map draws on the real onsen town of Yuzawa: the station, the bathhouses and inns on the slope, the cedars of the shrine, and the border tunnel that opens the book.

title: The Sound of the Mountain
author: Yasunari Kawabata
description: Kamakura, the old seaside capital, where one sleepless night the aging Shingo Ogata hears a deep sound from the wooded hills behind his house and takes it for a summons. He commutes to a Tokyo office along the line north, so the map runs from the temple town to the gardens of the capital.

title: The Sound of Waves
author: Yukio Mishima
description: Mishima's simple, luminous love story is set on Uta-jima, a small fishing island in Ise Bay drawn from the real island of Kamishima, where the young fisherman Shinji and the diver's daughter Hatsue fall in love against a tide of gossip. The whole island is the book: the fishing village and its harbour, the steep stone steps of the Yashiro shrine to the sea god, the lighthouse on the height, and the sea itself, worked by the boats and the diving women.

title: The Temple of the Golden Pavilion
author: Yukio Mishima
description: Mishima's novel reworks a real event: the burning of the Golden Pavilion, Kinkaku-ji, by a young acolyte monk in 1950. The stammering, ugly Mizoguchi comes from a poor coastal temple to serve at Rokuon-ji in Kyoto, and his worship of the pavilion's unbearable beauty curdles until he destroys it. The city is real throughout: the gilded pavilion above its pond, the temple grounds where he lodges, Otani University where he meets the crippled cynic Kashiwagi, and the wartime and postwar streets of Kyoto.

title: White Teeth
author: Zadie Smith
description: Smith's North West London is a working, multicultural map: the terraced streets of Willesden and Cricklewood where the Iqbal and Jones families make their tangled lives from 1975 to the millennium, the high roads and cafés where the men gather, the local school, and a final swerve to a genetics institute in the centre of town. The map runs from Willesden Green east across Cricklewood and Kilburn to the West End.

title: The Hostage
author: Zayd Mutee Dammaj
description: Yemen in the 1940s, under the rule of the Imamate. A boy from a highland tribe is held as a hostage for his family's loyalty and made a page-servant in the governor's fortress. The map runs from the mountain city of Taiz below Jabal Sabir north across the highlands to the imamic capital at Sana'a, roughly 250 kilometres away.

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
author: Zora Neale Hurston
description: Janie Crawford's search for love and a self of her own carries her across Florida through three marriages: from her grandmother's cabin and a loveless farm in the west, to the all-Black town of Eatonville where she is the mayor's silenced wife, to the Everglades 'muck' by Lake Okeechobee where she finds joy with Tea Cake, until the great 1928 hurricane. Hurston roots her landmark of Black American literature in real places she knew, above all the self-governing town of Eatonville and the migrant bean fields of the Glades.
